extracted.intended_audience: systematic review authors (particularly Cochrane review authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for defining pre-specified eligibility criteria (PICO and study designs) for intervention systematic reviews and for planning how studies and intervention variants will be grouped for synthesis (meta-analysis and other syntheses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-specify eligibility criteria based on PICO and study types
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility criteria should be based on the PICO elements of the review question plus a specification of the types of studies that have addressed these questions; systematic review authors should pre-specify criteria for including and excluding studies in the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions about which studies to include (and exclude), and how they will be combined in the review’s synthesis, should be documented and justified in the review protocol. Criteria should be set before knowing which studies will be included to reduce bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define the review PICO, PICO for each synthesis, and PICO of included studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish among (a) the review PICO (on which eligibility is based), (b) the PICO for each synthesis (the specific question each synthesis aims to answer), and (c) the PICO of the included studies (what was actually investigated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the review PICO and the PICO for each synthesis to specify eligible studies and plan syntheses; these should relate clearly to the review question/hypotheses. Plan grouping of variants of PICO elements with synthesis in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predefining unambiguous criteria for participants (MECIR C5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define in advance the eligibility criteria for participants in the studies. Predefined, unambiguous eligibility criteria are mandatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participant criteria should be sufficiently broad to encompass likely study diversity but narrow enough to yield a meaningful pooled answer. Consider setting, diagnosis/definition, demographic factors, and justify any restrictions to maintain global relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider when developing participant criteria (Box 3.2.a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how disease/condition is defined; key characteristics describing participants; relevant demographic factors; setting; who should make the diagnosis; other participant types to exclude; how studies with only a subset of eligible participants will be handled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid diagnostic criteria that would unnecessarily exclude older studies; consider participant-level vs study-level characteristics; plan strategies for partial overlap (e.g. majority rule, retrieve subgroup data, document decisions, run sensitivity analyses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Predefine strategy for studies with subset of eligible participants (MECIR C6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define in advance how studies that include only a subset of relevant participants will be addressed (e.g. when studies include both eligible and ineligible participants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify mechanisms to retrieve eligible-participant data where possible; if not possible, pre-specify sensible rules (avoid arbitrary cut-offs if data unavailable), document difficult decisions, consult advisory groups, and consider sensitivity analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define population characteristics that might modify intervention effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether there are population characteristics (e.g. severity, age groups) expected to modify effect size and plan to address these (restrict scope or investigate as subpopulations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If subpopulations are identified, either limit the scope of the review or maintain breadth and analyse subpopulations (preferably with a priori subgroup analyses stated in the protocol). Avoid splitting into too many subgroups that leave too few studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify and document any changes to eligibility criteria (MECIR C13)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any changes to eligibility criteria or outcomes must be justified and documented; post-hoc inclusion/exclusion decisions should keep faith with the objectives of the review, not be data-driven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not modify protocol eligibility on the basis of study findings or synthesis results. Sensible post-hoc decisions may be necessary but must be recorded and, where appropriate, accompanied by sensitivity analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predefine unambiguous criteria for interventions and comparators (MECIR C7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define in advance the eligible interventions and the interventions against which these can be compared in the included studies; this is mandatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about comparator types (inactive control vs active control). Predefine restrictions regarding delivery, dose, duration, intensity, co-interventions and other features. Consider exactly what is delivered, who delivers it, how, where, when, how much, and whether it can be adapted (use TIDieR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider when developing criteria for types of interventions (Box 3.2.b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask what the experimental and control interventions are; whether the intervention varies (dose, delivery, provider, frequency); whether all variations are included; whether studies including part of the intervention or co-interventions are included; consider meanings of 'control', 'placebo', 'usual care'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After broad definition, decide how variants will be handled in synthesis; judge whether differences are clinically important and may require separate groups or subgroup examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify intervention characteristics that may modify effects (Table 3.2.b Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select intervention characteristics that could importantly modify the size of the intervention effect, informed by content-specific literature and expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tools such as the TIDieR checklist or iCAT-SR for complex interventions to identify characteristics (what, who, when/how much). Consider mechanism of action when selecting characteristics to group by.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label and define intervention groups for synthesis (Table 3.2.b Step 2a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a short label and describe core characteristics used to assign interventions from included studies to groups (based on content, purpose/theory, mode, provider, dose, duration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on clinically meaningful groups that inform implementation; consider existing systems, provide examples for hard-to-describe groups, pilot criteria to ensure groups are distinct but not too narrow; logic models may help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define levels for groups based on dose or intensity (Table 3.2.b Step 2b)
rubrics_metrics.description: For groups defined by 'how much' of an intervention (dose/intensity), specify quantitative criteria for each level based on practice or rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use practical cut-offs (e.g. recommended intake, session length, frequency, intensity metrics); base levels on how interventions are used in practice or on mechanistic rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether existing taxonomy/systems exist for grouping interventions (Table 3.2.b Step 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess existing intervention taxonomies and frameworks for labelling and describing interventions and use them where appropriate rather than creating new groupings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer systems that use understandable terminology, are developed systematically with stakeholder input, and have been validated. Examples: BCT taxonomy, behaviour change wheel, ProFaNE taxonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan how specified intervention groups will be used in synthesis and reporting (Table 3.2.b Step 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to pool interventions in a single meta-analysis ('lumping') with subgroup exploration, or to perform separate syntheses ('splitting') for specific interventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice should be driven by the question of interest and clinical relevance. Document analytic approach in protocol and consider implications for interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide how to handle multi-component interventions (Table 3.2.b Step 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify how interventions with multiple components or co-interventions will be grouped or analysed (options include components-based meta-regression or network meta-analysis, grouping by main component, separate 'multi-component' group, study-by-study reporting, or exclusion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each option has trade-offs: components approaches may be challenging but informative; lumping multi-component interventions risks unexplained heterogeneity; excluding may reduce relevance. Pre-specify chosen approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build contingencies by specifying specific and broader intervention groups (Table 3.2.b Step 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan grouping at more than one level so that broader syntheses are possible if too few studies are identified for more specific groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This two-level approach provides flexibility: synthesize broad groups if necessary, and present specific-group analyses if sufficient data exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define comparisons for each planned synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: For each synthesis, specify which intervention groups will be compared (e.g. intervention vs placebo, intervention vs control, intervention A vs intervention B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard meta-analyses compare two groups at a time; plan which comparisons will form the basis of syntheses. Consider complexity for network meta-analysis separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcomes: select critical/important outcomes and avoid using outcomes as eligibility except when justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcomes usually are not eligibility criteria; include all outcomes likely to be meaningful and not trivial. Critical and important outcomes should be limited in number and include both adverse and beneficial outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A review may legitimately restrict eligibility to specific outcomes in some circumstances (e.g. reviews focused on adverse effects). Pre-specify primary and secondary outcomes in the protocol and limit number for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide which study designs to include and group by design features
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether to include randomized trials and/or non-randomized studies; eligibility should be based on explicit study design features (not inconsistent primary-study labels), and non-randomized studies should be grouped by design features reflecting inferential strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-randomized studies are appropriate when RCTs cannot address harms, long-term outcomes, specific populations, or when randomization is impossible. Plan whether to synthesize non-randomized and randomized studies together or separately and anticipate increased heterogeneity (use suitable meta-analytic models).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grouping study designs using a taxonomy (e.g. Cochrane NRS Methods Group)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a taxonomy of design features to group non-randomized studies expected to have similar inferential strength and provide consistent language for describing study design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions should be made for each type of non-randomized design and documented in the protocol; consider design-specific synthesis strategies (e.g. separate analyses, meta-regression).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include studies irrespective of publication status unless exclusion justified (MECIR C12)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies based on publication status only if explicitly justified; include unpublished, partially published, and grey literature where feasible to reduce publication bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtaining unpublished studies is challenging and they may be an unrepresentative subset, but excluding all unpublished studies is more likely to introduce bias. Consider resource implications and report rationale for any exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider language restrictions carefully with regard to bias and equity
rubrics_metrics.description: Review authors should consider implications for bias and equity if they restrict eligible studies to one language and be cautious because searching and analysing studies in all languages can be resource-intensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess trade-offs and document language restrictions and their justification in the protocol; consider impact on equity (see Chapter 16).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for missing or insufficient detail in study reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider and pre-specify how to categorise studies whose reports contain insufficient detail (e.g. insufficient intervention description or participant characteristics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilot criteria, use examples, attempt to contact study authors for clarification, and define conservative approaches for classification; record decisions and consider sensitivity analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan subgroup analyses a priori and report as objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Subgroup analyses should ideally be planned a priori and stated as secondary objectives in the protocol, not driven by data availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subgroup definitions should be specified in advance (including methods for participant-level vs study-level subgrouping) and be accompanied by rationale; post-hoc subgrouping risks bias and should be documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standardised terminology for interventions to aid comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Define intervention groups with standardised labels and descriptions to overcome varied descriptions by study authors and to enable comparison and synthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardization enables comparison of characteristics across studies (common features and differences) and consistent reporting. Consider using established taxonomies or provide clear operational definitions.
